promptText: In vector search, what fundamental problem does metadata filtering solve that similarity ranking alone cannot?
options: It restricts which vectors are even eligible for comparison, since cosine similarity has no concept of ownership, permissions, or recency
It improves embedding quality by adding extra dimensions to the vector
It makes the ANN index smaller by deleting irrelevant vectors permanently
It replaces the need for a reranker entirely
explanation: Cosine/vector similarity only measures semantic closeness; metadata filtering adds a separate, boolean eligibility check (tenant, access level, date) so an ineligible-but-semantically-close document never outranks a correctly scoped one.

promptText: Why can a naive post-filtering strategy (run ANN search, then discard non-matching candidates) return fewer than k results even when enough matching documents exist in the corpus?
options: The ANN index only ever returns k results total, so filtering always halves that number
The unfiltered top-N candidates it examined may simply not have included the sparse set of documents that satisfy a selective filter
Post-filtering always applies the wrong metadata field by default
Vector databases silently cap the number of filtered results to prevent overload
explanation: If the predicate is selective (e.g., a small tenant), the true matches may not be among the N geometrically closest vectors examined before filtering, so filtering afterward can discard almost everything and under-return.

promptText: Where should the mandatory tenant/access-control portion of a retrieval filter be derived from?
options: A client-supplied request parameter, validated on a best-effort basis
The authenticated identity resolved server-side (e.g., from the Spring Security context), never from client input
Whichever value produces the most retrieved documents
The document with the highest similarity score, applied retroactively
explanation: The chapter stresses that security-relevant filter fragments must be built server-side from verified identity; trusting a client-supplied tenant_id field is a classic cross-tenant privilege-escalation vulnerability.

promptText: What is the 'selectivity' of a metadata filter predicate?
options: The number of boolean operators (AND/OR) used in the predicate
The fraction of the corpus that satisfies the predicate
The latency added by evaluating the predicate
The number of distinct vector stores that support the predicate
explanation: Selectivity is defined as |{v in corpus : P(v) true}| / N — the single number that predicts which filtering strategy will behave well.

promptText: Why do HNSW-based vector indexes struggle more with arbitrary metadata filters than IVF-based indexes typically do?
options: HNSW graphs rely on shortcut edges assuming traversal can visit any node, and restricting traversal to a scattered eligible subset breaks those shortcuts, whereas IVF's cluster-list structure can more easily restrict which vectors within selected clusters are scored
HNSW does not support metadata at all, while IVF stores metadata natively in its graph edges
IVF indexes are always brute-force, so filtering is trivially free
HNSW graphs are rebuilt from scratch on every filtered query, unlike IVF
explanation: IVF's coarse cluster routing composes reasonably well with a predicate restricting which vectors within a cluster are scored; HNSW's navigable-graph shortcuts assume unrestricted traversal, so filtering requires more specialized 'filtered ANN' engineering.

promptText: Using the back-of-envelope model from the chapter, if a filter has selectivity s = 0.01 and you want k = 10 results via post-filtering, roughly how many unfiltered candidates N should you retrieve before filtering?
explanation: The inequality N ≥ k/s gives N ≥ 10/0.01 = 1,000 — a real latency and data-transfer cost that grows sharply as selectivity drops, motivating a switch to pre-filtering or filtered-ANN.

promptText: What distinguishes 'filtered ANN' (predicate-aware traversal) from naive pre-filtering when the eligible set is large?
options: Filtered ANN bakes predicate evaluation into the graph traversal itself and dynamically expands the search frontier until k eligible results are found, avoiding both the under-return risk of post-filtering and the brute-force fallback risk of naive pre-filtering
Filtered ANN always ignores the predicate for large eligible sets to preserve speed
Filtered ANN requires a separate database engine unrelated to the vector index
Filtered ANN can only be used when selectivity is exactly 1.0
explanation: Filtered ANN checks the predicate inline per visited node and keeps expanding the search rather than stopping at a fixed N, so it neither under-returns (like post-filtering) nor degrades to slow brute-force scanning of a large subset (like naive pre-filtering).

promptText: In a pgvector/Postgres-backed vector store, how does metadata filtering typically compose with the query itself?
options: It cannot be combined with vector search in the same query at all

The filter is translated into a native SQL WHERE predicate combined with the vector distance operator, letting Postgres's query planner decide whether to use a B-tree index or the vector index first based on selectivity estimates
Postgres always performs a full sequential scan regardless of any indexes present
pgvector requires a separate, unrelated database just for metadata
explanation: A pgvector query like SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY embedding <=> ? LIMIT k lets the ordinary Postgres planner combine predicates and vector search, inheriting decades of relational query-planner sophistication.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend allow-listing which metadata fields a client may filter on, rather than accepting an arbitrary client-constructed filter expression tree?
options: Allow-listing improves embedding quality

An unconstrained expression tree could reference security-critical fields (like tenant_id) or use OR/negation in ways that widen eligibility and bypass isolation, whereas an allow-list keeps the security-critical fragments structurally impossible for client input to touch
Vector stores technically cannot parse expression trees with more than one clause
Allow-listing is required only for range filters, never for equality filters
explanation: A client-crafted filter like 'tenant_id = other-tenant OR true' could bypass isolation entirely if the server didn't constrain which fields and operators a client may specify.

promptText: Why is it recommended to keep filter values as low-cardinality, normalized enums (e.g., ISO date formats, canonical tenant IDs) rather than free text?
options: Because metadata filters are almost always exact-match or range comparisons, and inconsistent values like 'Acme Corp' vs 'acme-corp' silently produce empty or incomplete results that look like retrieval bugs but are actually data-hygiene bugs
Because vector databases reject any field containing more than one distinct value
Because low-cardinality fields automatically improve embedding similarity scores
Because free text fields cannot be stored in a vector store's metadata payload at all
explanation: Filters are exact-match/range operations, not fuzzy text search, so inconsistent casing or synonyms for the same logical value silently fail to match, producing confusing empty-result bugs.

promptText: Why should hard security exclusions and soft ranking preferences (like deprioritizing stale content) be implemented as architecturally distinct mechanisms?
options: Because a filter either includes or excludes absolutely, while a soft preference should be a scoring adjustment applied after retrieval — conflating them risks either silently excluding relevant results or letting a good-enough semantic match bypass a security-critical exclusion
Because vector stores only support one mechanism at a time, never both
Because soft preferences are always more expensive to compute than hard filters
Because reranking can only operate on filtered fields, not on scores
explanation: The chapter's 'bouncer vs. judge' framing: hard exclusions (access control) must never be relaxed by relevance score, while soft preferences (like recency) should never be implemented as an absolute filter that could exclude a document that's the only available answer.

promptText: A team observes latency spikes for certain filter combinations even though their vector store advertises pre-filter support. What is the most likely root cause the chapter points to?
options: The filter occasionally matches a huge eligible set (e.g., 'all public documents'), triggering the store's brute-force or large-subset fallback path, which is far slower than either a small pre-filtered set or unfiltered ANN search
Pre-filtering strategies never have latency variance by design
The vector store is caching stale embeddings for all filtered queries
The reranker is being invoked twice for every filtered query
explanation: Pre-filtering's brute-force exact-search fallback is fast for small eligible sets but can become a latency cliff when a supposedly selective filter combination actually resolves to a large eligible set, especially as corpus size grows over time.

promptText: Why must recall@k be redefined once metadata filtering is part of a retrieval pipeline, according to the chapter's discussion of evaluation?
options: Recall@k should still be measured against the whole corpus's true nearest neighbors, ignoring the filter entirely

The meaningful denominator becomes the true nearest neighbors among ELIGIBLE documents only, since a semantically closer but ineligible document was never a candidate the system was supposed to surface
Recall@k becomes meaningless and should be replaced entirely by latency metrics
Recall@k should be computed once per vector store vendor, not per filter scenario
explanation: Measuring recall against unfiltered ground truth unfairly penalizes a correctly-filtered system for 'missing' documents it was never supposed to return; evaluation harnesses need per-filter-scenario ground truth among eligible documents.

promptText: In a system supporting a 'search only within a folder/workspace subtree' feature with arbitrarily nested folders, why does a naive folder_id = X equality filter fail to express 'search this whole subtree'?
options: Vector stores cannot store folder IDs as metadata

It only matches documents directly in folder X, not documents nested in descendant subfolders, so the common fix is to materialize a folder_path or ancestor-ID list at ingestion time to make the subtree query a single indexable predicate
Equality filters are always slower than range filters regardless of use case
Folder hierarchies cannot be represented in any metadata schema
explanation: A flat equality filter can't express hierarchy; materializing a path or ancestor-array at ingestion (accepting higher update cost when folders are re-parented) lets 'search the subtree' become one indexable predicate rather than a query-time tree walk.

promptText: During a migration window where old and new embedding-model vectors temporarily coexist in the same index, why must query-time filtering include an embedding_model_version predicate?
options: Because distances computed between embeddings from two different models are not meaningful — different models place semantically similar content at different points in incompatible vector spaces, so mixing them into one ranked list produces incomparable, misleading scores
Because vector stores charge extra for mixed-version indexes
Because old embeddings must always be physically deleted before any query can run
Because embedding_model_version filtering improves compression ratios during re-indexing
explanation: Cosine similarity between vectors from different embedding models is not a meaningful comparison; filtering to a single model version during the transition avoids silently mixing incomparable distance scores into one ranked result list.
